author.intro: The Relief of Chitral is the joint work of two brothers, “constantly being mistaken for one another”, as their Preface says, who were present together in the same campaign and both served in it as correspondents of The Times. George wrote the chapters on Sir Robert Low’s advance; Francis wrote the rest.

The first-hand history of the siege and relief of Chitral, 1895, in the complete text of the first edition.

In March 1895, deep in the Hindu Kush, the British Agent at Chitral and his escort were besieged in the fort of the Mehtars by the forces of Sher Afzul and Umra Khan of Jandul. Ninety-nine men of the 14th Sikhs and three hundred of the Kashmir Infantry under Captain Charles Vere Ferrers Townshend held the walls for forty-seven days against fire, sap and mine.

Two columns marched to their relief. Lieutenant-General Sir Robert Low led three brigades over the Malakand and through Swat and Dir; from Gilgit, Lieutenant-Colonel James Graves Kelly brought four hundred men of the 32nd Pioneers and two mountain guns across the snows of the Shandur Pass, the Pioneers carrying the guns themselves.

Written within months by two brothers who served in the campaign and reported it for The Times, The Relief of Chitral was greeted by The Spectator in November 1895: “To all who can enjoy military history this will be a fascinating book.”
